web_evidence.title: The Razor's Edge by W. Somerset Maugham
web_evidence.note: The complete primary text establishes a participating I-narrator from the Chapter One declaration that the book records his recollections through his meetings, actions, and final Chapter Seven account.

web_evidence.title: Somerset Maugham: Mirroring Human Life and Human Weaknesses
web_evidence.note: The scholarly article explicitly identifies The Razor's Edge as first-person narrative and explains that Maugham gathers information through personal contact with the characters.

web_evidence.title: Maugham's Half & Half
web_evidence.note: Gore Vidal's critical essay explicitly calls the book's narrator first-person and identifies the narrating character as Mr. Maugham.

web_evidence.title: The Razor's Edge Literary Devices
web_evidence.note: The structural analysis identifies fictional Maugham as the framing storyteller and distinguishes Larry's and Suzanne's first-person accounts as embedded narratives within that frame.

person_note: The controlling narrator is a fictionalized Somerset Maugham who participates as a peripheral witness, converses with the characters, and recounts his own observations and actions as I. Numerous first-person passages in the quote set belong instead to Larry, Suzanne, Isabel, or other speakers and were treated as local or embedded material. Maugham sometimes reconstructs unwitnessed scenes in third person and includes long embedded first-person accounts, but the complete text and structural sources show that these remain under his first-person frame rather than forming autonomous third-person sections; therefore the book is FIRST, not ALTERNATING. Remaining uncertainty is limited to a few Goodreads excerpts with stripped quotation marks, whose consequential attributions were resolved against the complete text.
